channel.description: New science of the mind, the universe and the tech that comes next.

item.title: Your brain isn't one organ. It's two.
item.description: Stanford researchers traced where the brain comes from and found two separate progenitor populations: Otx2+ cells build the forebrain and midbrain, Gbx2+ cells build the hindbrain, and they don't overlap from the earliest stages (mouse embryos). item.title: AI racing drone beat 3 world champion pilots: one camera, no GPS
item.description: MonoRace, from TU Delft's MAVLab, is an onboard AI drone racer that uses only a single rolling-shutter camera and an inertial sensor: no external motion tracking, no stereo cameras, no GPS. A neural network segments the race gates for state estimation, and a small network running on the flight controller sends motor commands directly at 500 Hz. item.title: Minds vs. Machines: 4 New Studies That Change How We Think
item.description: A single brain cell with 70 cm of wiring. A kind of selfishness that spreads. An AI that makes you an expert until it's taken away. And a hidden confidence dial inside language models. Four peer-reviewed studies from autumn 2026, explained with original 3D visuals.

item.title: Scientists watched a single quantum of sound jump
item.description: Quantum mechanics says vibration comes in discrete packets (phonons), but measuring an object's position can't reveal that. A Stanford-led team dispersively coupled a superconducting qubit to a lithium-niobate nanomechanical resonator (mechanical lifetime about 2.1 ms) and made repeated quantum non-demolition measurements of the phonon number. item.title: AI language models have a hidden confidence dial that decides when they answer
item.description: Do language models actually use their own confidence when deciding whether to answer or abstain? Researchers from Google DeepMind and Princeton built a four-phase test. Models applied an implicit threshold to internal confidence when abstaining. item.title: A planet was hiding in Webb's data
item.description: To photograph an exoplanet you have to subtract the glare of its star, but tiny telescope instabilities leave residual starlight behind. A team from Northwestern, Caltech, MIT and STScI built a physics-based starlight model, optimising millions of parameters with automatic differentiation to compensate for those instabilities. item.title: ChatGPT made them better at data science, until it was taken away
item.description: In a randomized controlled trial, 487 management consultants were given ChatGPT access and training and asked to solve data-science tasks outside their skill set, tasks ChatGPT could not solve on its own. item.title: Could Webb's Densest Star Clusters Forge Black Holes?
item.description: The James Webb Space Telescope, helped by gravitational lensing, has resolved compact young star clusters in galaxies seen less than a billion years after the Big Bang: the Cosmic Gems arc and the Firefly Sparkle. item.title: The Solar System may fall apart much sooner than we thought
item.description: Earlier models treated the Sun's future mass loss as smooth and found the planets' orbits stay stable far beyond the age of the universe. A Caltech-led study instead models it as random puffs of ejected mass, each giving the planets a small kick. item.title: 4 Discoveries From Autumn 2026 That Rewire How We See Reality
item.description: A star with no fusion inside, a brain that's secretly two organs, a third kind of magnet, and a fear response that blurs reality on purpose. Four peer-reviewed discoveries from autumn 2026, explained with original 3D visuals.

item.title: Critical PHP vulnerability: one web request can leave a ghost behind (update now)
item.description: On 21 October 2026 the PHP project shipped fixes for two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2. In the first (CVE-2026-109618), running out of memory can interrupt PHP while request data is only partly initialised, and cleanup may then treat it as valid. item.title: One mouse neuron, 70 cm of wiring: the brain's alertness system mapped
item.description: Allen Institute researchers mapped the locus coeruleus, the tiny brainstem 'blue spot' that makes noradrenaline (alertness, attention, stress), in mice. They imaged nearly 35,000 of its neurons across the whole brain and fully reconstructed dozens of them: the average axon is about 35 cm long, and one reached 70.32 cm of total branched length inside a mouse brain about 1 cm long. item.title: A Robot Knee-Jerk Reflex With No Sensor or Chip
item.description: Tohoku University engineers built a reflex for robot muscles out of air, a mechanical valve and a string. When an artificial muscle is stretched past a set length, a parallel "spindle" muscle pulls a string that opens the valve, and the muscle contracts. No electronic sensor or chip is involved. item.title: Fear makes your brain blur danger and safety
item.description: McGill researchers put mice in an augmented-reality arena that could switch instantly between a 'danger' and a 'safety' context, while miniature microscopes recorded hundreds of neurons in the ventral hippocampus. item.description: Radio telescopes caught Betelgeuse changing shape in step with a suspected companion star. Using the VLA and ALMA at seven frequencies (22–485 GHz) from 2021 to 2026, a team led by MIT Haystack Observatory with the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian mapped the red supergiant's extended atmosphere: gas near 3,500 K at about 2.7 stellar radii, cooling to about 2,220 K closer in. item.title: Webb found a star with no fusion inside
item.description: JWST spotted MoM-BH*-1 at cosmic dawn, a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. It looks like a star but puts out ~100 billion times more energy than any star could. The team's best explanation is a black hole of ~100,000 solar masses wrapped in a dense gas cocoon about the size of our solar system: a 'black hole star', where the light comes from accretion, not fusion. item.title: The "Lonely" Sleep Waves of the Aging Brain
item.description: During deep sleep, large groups of neurons go quiet and switch back on together, and these slow waves travel across the brain from front to back. A UC Berkeley team compared overnight EEG in 61 young and 75 older adults. item.title: A Neural Network That Computes With Light in a Fiber
item.description: Researchers at the University of Tokyo and NTT built a neural network around a single loop of optical fiber. Light pulses circling the loop do the computing. Their new training method, state-skipping direct feedback alignment, learns from the final error and never needs to read the loop's hidden states. item.title: How an Octopus Pours Itself Through a Tiny Hole
item.description: How does a soft animal with eight arms get its whole body through a hole narrower than the gap between its eyes? Researchers filmed three common octopuses crossing a clear partition 30 times. Every pass followed the same order: probe with one arm, push 3–5 arms through, then anchor and pull.
